blocks.text: See Matth. in VII. and XII, 34. and XXIII, 33. Luc. III, 7.

Saadia puts this very افعي [afʿī] for the Hebrew אפעה in his Arabic translation of Isaiah, Chapter XXX, 6. LIX, 5. That افعي [afʿī] is the viper is also confirmed by the testimony of Forsskål, who in the Materia Medica Cahirina at the end of the Descriptio Animalium, p. 142, likewise has Vipera, with the Arabic name افعي [afʿī], Ephe, added. — Shaw in his Travels, p. 159 of the German trans., mentions a serpent of the viper or snake kind, a foot long, whose colour varies with the soil in which it hides, called Leffah by the Arabs of western Africa. Oedmann (Fasc. 4, Chapter 8, p. 79) thinks this name is the Arabic افعي [afʿī] itself with the article prefixed. But this opinion seems hardly probable to me, since Shaw states expressly that the name means to burn in Arabic. From this it is clear that it must be written in Arabic letters لفاح [laffāḥ], from لفح [lafaḥa], fire burned with its heat, poison with its sharpness, whence the adjective لافح [lāfiḥ] burning. The serpent's name لفّاح [laffāḥ], however, is not found in the lexicons.

The أفعي [afʿī] of the Arabs is without doubt the Coluber Vipera of Hasselquist (Travels, p. 363), who described this serpent most accurately. I shall extract only a little. "Head slightly depressed on top, strongly depressed between the eyes [III, 129], strongly protruding at the sides and raised from the body. — Tail below the anus conical, short, tapering, ending at the tip in a slightly curved spine. — In Egypt everything that the pharmacopoeias require from the viper is taken from this: salt of viper, dried viper flesh, viper troches are all prepared from it, both for the use of the inhabitants and for export to Europe." — Niebuhr in the Preface to the Description of Arabia, p. XL, mentions a certain serpent called Afa by the Arabs, about which the inhabitants of those regions tell many fables. Oedmann (Fasc. 4, Chapter 8, p. 78) takes this serpent for our أفعي [afʿī]; but the spelling does not agree, for Niebuhr writes the name Äfae as افاة [afāh]. Moreover, what the Arabs relate of the Afa, that it kills by its hiss alone, agrees better with the fables of the ancients about the basilisk. See Bochart below, Chapter IX.
That these stories about vipers are fables is shown by Buffon's continuator, de La Cépède, vol. 2, Hist. Nat. des Serpens, p. 35.

Albert Schultens inquired more precisely into the origin and various meanings of the verb فعي [faʿā] in his Notes on the Hamasa Anthology, appended to Erpenius's Grammar, pp. 420–421. From the Arab lexicographers he shows that فعي [faʿā] properly means he blew with puffed-out mouth, whence it is used of a woman in labour who, having long held her breath, at last, overcome by pain, bursts out with a gasping cry.
This artful etymology seems unnecessary. The viper seems to have been given the name אפעה, افعي [afʿī] from hissing and from blowing with open, or rather puffed-out, mouth.
